Industrial robots are increasingly prevalent in machining, driven by their ability to deliver high dexterity and cost-efficiency. Nevertheless, inherent deformations stemming from machining forces, their own weight, and operating conditions often impair robot performance and output. To address this, this study introduces a new method for estimating robot end-effector deformation, leveraging a data-driven approach that relies solely on acceleration data from an EasySense inertial measurement unit (IMU). This technique eliminates the need for external force/torque sensors, strain gauges, or complex structural models. A support vector regression algorithm is trained to map recorded vibrations to deformation amounts, using data collected from a KUKA robot equipped with a 3-axis force/torque sensor across various loads and workpieces. Results indicate that the IMU-driven model achieves an average positioning accuracy of 0.51 mm, representing a 40% improvement over prior IMU-based methods. This proposed framework offers a cost-effective solution for precise deformation compensation in mass-production machining environments.

Early life experiences significantly influence long-term health outcomes. This paper introduces a longitudinal modeling framework designed to capture these influences and assess their evolving impacts across time. We formulate the problem using a hierarchical linear model, where the random effects and their temporal evolution are defined by a Gaussian Process. A key advantage of this approach is its flexibility in incorporating diverse covariates, including non-linear features. Through simulations and real-world longitudinal analysis, we demonstrate the model's effectiveness.

A standard approach for computing electronic integrals in polyatomic systems involves using overlapped grid points combined with different atomic basis function sets under the assumption that, in a localized atomic framework, total energy can be derived from a sum of contributions from individual atoms. Under this condition, it is customary to employ different integration routines tailored to specific atomic environments. Originally, total energy derivation required solving a boundary value problem to determine grid point weights tailored to each molecule; however, recent work has demonstrated that weights can be efficiently calculated using existing software without modification. This study extends that methodology to include exponents and coefficients within the basis functions. When applied in conjunction with an atomic partitioning strategy, such as the Becke method, the resulting framework enables the parallel computation of electronic integrals across varying subsets of grid points.

In the graph $G$, a subset $S \subseteq V(G)$ is termed a resolving set if, for any distinct vertices $x$ and $y$ in $G$, the sum of their distances to each member of $S$ varies (i.e., $\sum_{s \in S} d(x,s) \neq \sum_{s \in S} d(y,s)$). A minimum resolving set corresponds to the graph's dimension, denoted as $dim(G)$. While the concept was originally introduced by O. O'Keefe and K. R. Bailey, this study explores a specific variant where $S$ is constrained to be an independent set, thereby establishing sufficient criteria and determining the precise values for the circular, grid, wheel, crown, path, and complete bipartite graphs, along with several other structures.

Powerdomains serve as the topos underpinning the type system of nondeterministic functions within the untyped lambda calculus, particularly for those without recursion. In an earlier work, Bucci, Koutzianas, and Ziliani introduced a variant for finite power that is both orthogonal and fully abstract for call-by-name recursion schemes, extending the concept to include probabilistic nondeterminism. Subsequent unrecursion-based versions were developed by Bucci and Zili in separate works to cover call-by-value semantics. In contrast, this paper delivers a new formulation of finite powerdomain that is fully abstract for call-by-value recursion schemes; notably, one of its underlying components is the set of finite partial functions. Additionally, the authors provide operational and denotational semantics for a simply typed language incorporating both probabilistic behavior and nondeterminism within the call-by-value framework for recursion schemes. Finally, the authors demonstrate that their proposed powerdomain achieves orthogonality and full abstractness by establishing an operational/semantic correspondence for these recursion schemes in call-by-value.

We present a one-dimensional climate model designed to simulate hothouse atmospheres, which incorporates both radiative-convective equilibrium and radiative transfer. This framework models a dynamic hydrologic cycle driven by the self-consistent solution of cloud microphysical processes. In hothouse conditions, this cycle operates under an extreme regime distinct from typical Earth-like scenarios, characterized by a single dominant convection cell that extends from the substellar point down to the night-side substellar point. The paper analyzes the stability of this saturated climate state against dry perturbations, incorporating the effects of cloud macrophysical processes. Our findings indicate a cloud formation process, which is consistent with prior literature, yet we observe that this mechanism also plays a role in the same physics described in the abstract, highlighting the dynamic nature of these systems.

This approach yields a consistent projective twistor space formulation for the resulting field-theoretic systems. By formulating the dynamics of these systems as differential equations, we achieve an explicit representation of their solutions. Furthermore, our analysis recovers the standard description of SDYM self-duality in four-dimensional Minkowski spacetime as a specific limit. In that limit, our higher-spin structure naturally generates the corresponding finite-dimensional non-Abelian Higgs doublet.

Data-intensive fields like medical image classification encounter substantial challenges stemming from the expensive and time-consuming nature of data acquisition and annotation. However, image labeling frequently suffers from noise, which can have detrimental impacts on model performance. Although data augmentation techniques have traditionally been employed to simulate such noise, they often fail to capture the specific noise patterns of a particular domain. This paper introduces a labeling augmentation approach using generative adversarial networks (GANs) to generate synthetic noisy labels, effectively simulating real-world imperfect annotation scenarios. Our method involves two primary stages: first, transferring the semantic information from rigid transformations to a generator; second, using a discriminator to guide the creation of soft labels that reflect realistic imperfect hardness based on the first stage's outputs. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing augmentation strategies, yielding improvements of 1.6% to 2.2% on average across four abdominal CT datasets when evaluated against state-of-the-art models.

Experimental measurements of the skin-friction drag coefficient were obtained using torque balance methods across a range of flow speeds in smooth rectangular channels. These experiments covered fully developed turbulent flow at constant mass flux up to the fully rough regime, extending from the transition point and covering a wide spectrum of geometric and flow Reynolds numbers. The results align well with the recently proposed skin-friction law for smooth pipes, which posits that the drag coefficient depends on both Reynolds and geometric Reynolds numbers. Furthermore, the study presents the first experimental data on skin-friction coefficients in these conditions within the fully rough and developing flow regimes.

We introduce a novel method for linearizing yield conditions within amorphous solids, specifically accounting for plastic shear bands that exhibit non-uniform orientations relative to the surrounding elastic matrix. This approach relies on a newly derived class of screening equations governing the mechanical stresses generated by localized shear bands under elastic deformation. Unlike strong screening seen in granular matter, our findings identify a regime of weak screening that permits analytical solutions to a localized version of Biot's theory, similar to linear elasticity models. This technique successfully incorporates strongly screened shear bands into discontinuous plasticity theories and correctly captures key nonlinear elastic characteristics observed in experiments, such as abrupt jumps in acoustic wave velocities and the emergence of negative elastic wave modes upon yielding. Furthermore, these results indicate that yield surfaces for materials with strong screening behave similarly to those without such materials, expanding and refining the Burt-McCallum theory by incorporating the effects of localized shear bands and their associated localized strain fields.

Sgr A East is a supernova remnant (SNR) situated within the Galactic Center region. This study presents a new determination of the SNR's age, utilizing the X-ray data from the XMM-Newton observatory. We conducted a multi-wavelength analysis of the SNR by combining XMM-Newton observations with previously available data from the VLA and IRAS. We applied the GR17 model—a supernova shock model developed by [Guo et al. 2017]—to fit the multi-energy band X-ray spectra. We then compared these model predictions against non-thermal radio emission data from the VLA to refine our SNR age estimate. We found that the best-fit model corresponds to an age between 10 and 20 thousand years, which aligns well with prior research findings.

This study examines how local news coverage of COVID-19 correlated with infection and mortality rates across 100 U.S. communities. Initially, reporting was inconsistent, but it became inversely proportional to hospitalization rates and declined over time in relation to death rates. Regional coverage was heavily skewed toward severe cases, disproportionately impacting areas with older populations, low testing frequency, and high minority populations. Local reporting dynamics appeared independent of national reporting trends. Furthermore, extensive news coverage was linked to behavioral responses, including heightened social distancing, reduced mobility, improved hygiene, and mask usage. Conversely, intense reporting drove down demand for COVID-19 tests, hospital admissions, and emergency department visits. Overall, news coverage played a pivotal role in shaping public behavior.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) is celebrated for its flexibility in modeling complex physical phenomena. However, prior to 2004, its application to astrophysics was hindered by doubts regarding its capacity to accurately conserve mass, momentum, and energy. This paper demonstrates that such conservation is indeed achievable, provided that specific conditions are met. These conditions entail: (1) employing a momentum equation that incorporates a consistent SPH equation of state and interaction term; (2) utilizing energy conservation laws that follow directly from the momentum and mass equations; and (3) ensuring that all discrete forms of the governing equations remain consistent with one another. While these theoretical requirements were eventually met by a smoothed profile-based SPH energy conservation approach in 2004, our analysis shows that this method contains inherent flaws. Consequently, even the most recent SPH configurations fail to conserve energy when numerical dissipation or artificial viscosity is activated.

The interaction of real and virtual photons with nucleons is investigated, emphasizing the $Q^2$ behavior of the $G_E/G_M$ ratio and its influence on longitudinal spin polarization transfer. This study extends beyond the traditional $Q^2$ dependence of transverse polarization to explicitly incorporate $Q^2$-dependent longitudinal polarization in both the transverse and total spin sectors. This approach is achieved by deriving and utilizing a comprehensive spin four-vector framework, which accounts for the non-zero longitudinal polarization of the outgoing proton in deeply inelastic scattering (DIS) and enables a more accurate description of the transverse polarization of either incoming or outgoing nucleons in proton-proton collisions. Consequently, this formalism allows for the first time a unified description of the transverse polarization of interacting prons and the non-trivial $Q^2$ evolution of longitudinal polarization within the same theoretical structure.

Addressing the challenge of data-efficient learning, particularly in complex environments like robotics, we introduce an approach that leverages generative models of transitions to create synthetic training examples. Our method employs a learned mapping from the space of states to the space of actions to synthesize trajectories. We establish theoretical conditions under which utilizing these synthetic trajectories remains compatible with the training process. Theoretical findings are further supported by experiments demonstrating improved data efficiency across various domains in both reinforcement learning and imitation.

This study investigates non-resonant Higgs-Higgs ($HH)$ production via vector boson fusion in proton-proton collisions, focusing on the decay channel $HH \to b\bar{b}b\bar{b})$. Using an effective-field-theory framework, we establish constraints on the coupling $k_\lambda$ (relative to Standard Model expectations) derived from 13 TeV LHC data collected in 2016 and 2017. Our findings indicate that the observed upper limits align well with Standard Model predictions at the 95% confidence level. Additionally, we analyze the sensitivity of this search to complex-phase components within $k_\lambda$, which could signal Higgs boson mixing and imply CP violation.

Detecting the directional nature of nuclear recoils is a highly desirable outcome in the search for both dark matter and neutrinos. In the dark matter domain, it would allow scientists to distinguish potential signals from the overwhelming background generated by other nuclear recoils. For neutrino research, it would significantly enhance the study of the "neutrino floor," which is traditionally obscured by gamma and beta backgrounds. Over the past few decades, several experiments have been developed to achieve this directional detection. This review outlines the current state of these efforts and their prospects, with a specific focus on techniques that utilize ionization trails left by electrons. We explore two primary methods: the measurement of drifting electron avalanches (known as TPC with PAM or Time-Projection Chamber with PAM) and the tracking of faint, sub-luminous electron scintillations (known as CRESST technology). We also briefly mention alternative approaches used to achieve this goal.

Commercial driving operations are heavily influenced by external contextual factors such as traffic, weather, and road conditions, which can trigger unsafe behaviors. Consequently, monitoring these contexts is vital for enhancing commercial vehicle safety. This study proposes a novel approach to tracking driving contexts using data from vehicle-mounted sensors, specifically leveraging a combination of GPS location and acceleration data. The research presents two key contributions: first, a data-driven technique for selecting optimal contextual checkpoints along routes, and second, a method for classifying driving contexts based on vehicle dynamics at these points. This classification utilizes supervised learning on features derived from short-duration acceleration signals to distinguish between different driving conditions. To validate the approach, the study employs public datasets containing telemetry from multiple trucks, analyzing segments annotated by fleet managers to represent various commercial driving contexts.

Random fields, widely employed across disciplines like geostatistics, image analysis, and machine learning to represent random functions and their realizations, often necessitate intricate statistical dependencies. This paper introduces a novel class of random fields that exhibit intricate, clustered correlation patterns. Leveraging an underlying point process, we construct a binary matrix representing potential interactions, where the field's values are determined by multivariate Gaussian distributions conditioned on these interactions. These correlations naturally cluster around high-potential regions while decaying toward areas of low potential. Although the resulting correlation structure is complex, the conditional Gaussian distribution remains a simple linear function of nearby potential points, facilitating efficient computation. To demonstrate their utility, we apply these fields to simulate a real-world image featuring sparse objects set against a noisy background.

A graph $G$ with at least three vertices is defined as panccyclic if it contains cycles of every length from 3 to $n$ (the order). While edge connectivity conditions for this property have been extensively studied, those regarding vertex connectivity remain largely unexplored. This work establishes sufficient conditions ensuring a Hamiltonian graph is panccyclic and identifies specific scenarios where these conditions guarantee cycles of all lengths from 5 to $n$. Our key findings indicate that a Hamiltonian, $(a,b)$-traceable (a special subclass of graphs where the longest path is of length $n$) with vertex connectivity $\kappa(G) \ge (2/3)n - (5/9)$ possesses cycles of all lengths from 5 to $n$. These results are optimal in several instances. Additionally, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for a traceable graph to have paths of all lengths from 4 to $n$ based on its vertex connectivity $\kappa(G)$.

Our findings indicate a correlation between the directed flow of light hadrons and the nucleon spin-isospin asymmetry of nucleon-nucleon (NN) and meson-baryon (M-B) cross-sections. This behavior is linked to NN and MB scattering processes. The spin-isospin asymmetry in light hadron production is a key factor in explaining the directed flow. Time integration algorithms are essential for advancing solutions in systems governed by ordinary differential equations, particularly within the context of ordinary and partial differential equations. While numerous methods exist, many suffer from high computational costs due to high dimensionality. This study introduces a novel approach, the sparse-grid-based ASK algorithm, which leverages adaptive sampling of system states. The method utilizes the analytic structure of the solution to construct an explicit solution model via the Runge-Kutta framework on an adaptive sparse grid. The authors demonstrate that this algorithm achieves superior performance in terms of both computational efficiency and accuracy, particularly for multi-dimensional problems. The method is validated against an extended Fisher-Kolmogorov equation, a task known for its computational intensity, and a comparative analysis with standard Runge-Kutta methods and the ASK-2 algorithm reveals significant efficiency improvements. The authors also discuss the method's scalability and its potential to be applied to further problems.

This study focuses on extracting microscopic characteristics of a double delta potential by analyzing its resonance parameters. While quantum resonance parameters for a single delta well have been previously solved analytically, this work provides exact solutions for both the real and imaginary components of the resonance energy in a configuration with two deltas via straightforward algebraic methods. These findings are subsequently applied to define the concepts of resonant width and lifetime, which are then evaluated numerically for hydrogen molecules containing delta potentials modeled as effective nuclear short-range potentials.

This study examines the derivation of optimal paths within the Schr\"odinger bridge problem, focusing on the influence of degenerate states on the corresponding backward equation, a phenomenon that can arise from specific choices of a cost function or initial distribution. The analysis identifies such degenerate scenarios by determining the equation's solutions under a backward perspective, a method complemented by an examination of a nonlinear operator's differentiability with respect to a distributional input. The authors demonstrate that under particular constraints on the cost function, certain regions of the domain will inevitably become subject to a zero measure. The study further establishes that a necessary condition ensuring non-degenerate outcomes involves the inclusion of a strictly positive term within the cost function. Additionally, the findings indicate that even a minimal deviation from equilibrium stability—represented by a perturbation in the initial distribution—can trigger degeneracy.

The cross-section $\sigma_{t\bar{t}}$ for inclusive production of top-quark pairs is determined using a dataset of $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 5.02$ TeV, gathered by the CMS detector at the LHC with an integrated luminosity of $13.6 \, \mathrm{pb}^{-1}$. Analysis of dilepton events, characterized by two charged leptons of opposite sign in the final state with missing transverse momentum from neutrinos, is performed using both di-muon and di-electron channels. The measurement is restricted to events where the two leading jets each possess a transverse momentum exceeding the top-quark mass and the two leading b-jets exceed the expected bottom-quark mass. Under these kinematic requirements, the observed event yield is compared against predictions derived from next-to-leading-order (NLO) QCD simulations. Systematics related to the detector response, as well as theoretical uncertainties regarding the simulation modeling, are evaluated and incorporated into the final result. The resulting inclusive cross-section is measured as $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 7.71 \pm 0.22 \, (\mathrm{stat.}) \pm 0.41 \, (\mathrm{syst.}) \, \mathrm{pb}$. This value aligns well with NLO QCD calculations and is consistent with previous measurements obtained at higher center-of-mass energies.

This study examines the time-dependent behavior of a central degree of freedom interacting with a many-body localized (MBL) environment. We analyze systems where coupling is both two- and three-site extensive, demonstrating that one can distinguish between three distinct regimes: (i) the quasi-isolated case where the core dynamics mimic a single particle in MBL, (ii) a many-body induced-thermalization scenario where coupling creates effective interactions, (iii) the relaxation into an MBL phase. We identify the key parameters that differentiate these behaviors and analyze the system's properties within the fully thermalizing regime. Ultimately, our results suggest that the three-dof coupling offers the most robust representation of an effective bath, prompting future investigations into the non-equilibrium thermodynamics of central spins within many-body localized settings.

Conditions derived by the relationship between two sets of generalized Bessel functions, $J_{\mu_1,v_1,w_1}^{\alpha_1,\rho_1}(\cdot)$ and $J_{\mu_2,v_2,w_2}^{\alpha_2,\rho_2}(\cdot)$, are examined. Specifically, we present two sufficient conditions under which $J_{\mu_1,v,w}^{\alpha,\rho}(x)$ yields a subordination to $J_{\mu_2,v_2,w_2}^{\alpha_2,\rho_2}(x^{\alpha_2,\rho_2})$ when considering functions of a linear variable $ax+c$. Additionally, we explore sufficient criteria for establishing that $J_{\mu_1,v,w}^{\alpha,\rho}(x^{\alpha,\rho})p(z)$ is subordinate to $Ap(z^{\alpha,\rho})+Cp(z^{\alpha,\rho})$, where $A$ and $B$ are complex constants. Finally, we highlight several important consequences of our findings, demonstrating their potential utility for future research.

Urban physical contacts and social networking are pivotal drivers of economic output, innovation, and social advancement. While the significance of these in-person encounters is widely acknowledged, quantifying their precise economic value remains a complex challenge. This study leverages mobile device data to model city-level contact patterns across four major metropolitan areas, employing machine learning techniques to measure city-specific variations in contact frequency, spatial density, and mobility. Our analysis uncovers distinct differences in the efficiency of urban mixing and highlights a non-linear relationship: as city size expands, the rate of physical mixing initially accelerates before eventually plateauing. We employ these contact metrics as a foundational input for an econometric model assessing the value of urban mixing, which demonstrates a consistent positive correlation between higher contact frequencies and increased productivity.

This work introduces a two-step field-split nonlinear preconditioner designed to address two-phase flow and transport challenges. It demonstrates that this approach yields superior performance compared to traditional real pressure/saturation split nonlinear preconditioners. The proposed method begins with a nonlinear solve utilizing a conventional fully coupled Jacobian, from which the resulting transformed fields are utilized to generate a second preconditioned nonlinear system using a field-split strategy. A key study of a domain decomposition variant of this method is conducted, which establishes the domain decomposition field-split preconditioner as both robust and cost-effective. A numerical experiment validates these findings, confirming that this preconditioner achieves a more efficient solution strategy than its domain-independent counterpart.

Distinguishing chiral enantiomers through the use of chiral light is a critical challenge in the field. We introduce a highly efficient and all-chiral design for a cavity capable of generating chiral light, which effectively isolates enantiomers of molecules that show weak interaction with chiral light. This cavity is engineered using a helical arrangement of chiral metasurfaces, enabling strong coupling with an excitonic transition in a dissimilar chiral cavity quantum electrodics setup. Our findings demonstrate that this system produces a maximum differential vacuum splitting of 1.8 femtoseconds in the visible spectrum, surpassing previous results by a factor of 100. Additionally, the system achieves a peak differential cavity Q-factor of 1.8 × 10⁴ in the near-infrared range. These advancements promise to substantially enhance the sensitivity of detectors for chiral light.

This paper investigates the partition functions of Jackiw-Teitelboi (JT) gravity and two-dimensional string theory formulated on four-manifolds with non-trivial boundaries. We demonstrate that the boundary contributions to the path integral actions and corresponding amplitudes are identical in both frameworks. Consequently, we establish that two-dimensional string theory with compactified matter is equivalent to a dilaton-tuned version of RTJ gravity. This equivalence allows for the computation of string theory partition functions using BTI gravity methods. Specifically, we analyze cases where the boundary represents the sphere topology, deriving results for both string theories. Our findings for this calculation match those previously obtained in the context of island formation. This outcome further corroborates the validity of the concept of islands.

The Alcubierre metric defines a spacetime geometry that permits a particle to experience zero acceleration while seemingly traveling faster than light, as an extensive acceleration horizon forms ahead of the mass in motion. To achieve this, a specific function, or shift vector, must be carefully constructed. Although the mass resides within the shift's region of effect, the necessary energy to sustain the metric is typically associated with the mass's location. This metric is currently considered the sole viable candidate for superluminal travel, and its viability hinges entirely on the existence of a solution to the Einstein field equations. This study examines a unique configuration of the Alcubierre metric where the relationship between the energy and the effect is spatially reversed, placing the mass at the source of the effect and the energy within the mass's location. By doing so, I present a specific metric that is theoretically consistent with Einstein's equations under these inverted conditions.

Urban centers face the challenge of maintaining and repairing their aging underground infrastructure, such as sewers and subways. Ineffective upkeep can lead to safety hazards and exorbitant operational expenses. To address these issues, we present a new methodology for managing subterranean systems. Our approach utilizes a 3D information model that integrates data from diverse sources to create a unified digital representation. This document details the application of our technique to a subway system and a sewer network, and we evaluate it by examining how digital twins can support the upkeep of underground facilities. Our findings indicate that implementing this 3D information model enhances maintenance processes and allows for better resource allocation.

We investigate the transverse spin dephasing of a single electron coupled to two-dimensional Wigner crystal ions via Ising interactions. By applying the high-temperature approximation, we map this system onto an effective model featuring random antiferromagnetic couplings. We analyze both the static behavior and the subsequent dynamical evolution of the electron's coherent phase. Additionally, we examine the transition from coherent to incoherent dephasing regimes as functions of both the electron-to-ion mass ratio and the coupling strength.

Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS) is a powerful imaging technique for analyzing nanoscale surface properties. However, the underlying mechanisms driving signal amplification remain elusive. This study employs finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations to dissect the contributions of tip-enhanced scattering and the nanoscale optical "antenna" effect. Our results demonstrate that both phenomena significantly boost tERS signals, with the tip's electromagnetic radiation directly scattered by the sample accounting for a major portion of the enhancement. To isolate these local effects, researchers must utilize specialized experimental configurations. To clarify the distinct roles of these mechanisms, simulations were conducted examining the influence of various experimental parameters, the spatial distribution of electric field enhancements, and systems incorporating realistic nonlinear cross-section values. Ultimately, simulations using realistic nonlinear values indicate that the antenna effect is substantially less potent than previously assumed.

This study introduces a new 40 GHz survey of the Galactic Center, conducted to investigate Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). The survey achieved a sensitivity of 1.5 mJy/beam and a velocity resolution of 10.5 km/s. Initial findings indicate that among 119 observed sources, 13 exhibit significant detections (above 4 sigma), 19 show moderate detections (above 3 sigma), and 80 are undetected. Velocity-integrated flux densities for detected sources are generally in the range of 10 to 200 mJy km/s, with a few exceptions exceeding 300 mJy km/s. The spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of AME candidates are generally flatter than those of molecular clouds, often failing to align with standard cloud emission models. Furthermore, a correlation exists between the line intensity and spectral index, suggesting that AME originates from non-thermal sources rather than typical clouds. The study also notes a strong relationship between the intensity and spectral index of AME candidates and the lines of sight toward low-latitude Galactic plane sources. These results support the hypothesis that AME arises from non-thermal processes, potentially involving lines of sight toward low-latitude galactic plane sources. Ammonium sulfate (NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$ (Nut) is a prototypical AII proton-conducting ferroelectric material. Its diverse functionalities—including proton conductivity, antiferroelectricity, and optical activity—stem from the behavior of mobile protons located between sulfate layers. This material features multiple ferroelectric and antiferroelectric phases that can be manipulated via temperature and pressure. This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the structural evolution of Nut under varying external fields. The results indicate that both pressure and temperature can be used to tune the ratio of $N$H$_2$ to $N$H$^+$ groups on the ammonium cation. This adjustment drives structural phase transitions between different ferroelectric and antiferroelectric phases. The computational results are consistent with previous experimental observations.

Probabilistic learning tasks often elicit either a maximization strategy, where agents select the most probable option, or a matching strategy, where they distribute choices according to the observed distribution. Previous research indicates that both humans and animals can exhibit matching behavior beyond what reinforcement learning predicts, though the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the cognitive processes underlying probabilistic matching in humans, specifically determining its relationship with reinforcement learning and exploring the neural mechanisms involved. We hypothesized that while maximization results from a learned value representation, matching reflects a direct, non-inferred representation of probabilities. To test this, we employed a within-subjects design where participants performed probabilistic tasks under both maximization and matching conditions in separate sessions. Results showed that while prior experience driven reinforcement learning accounted for most of the maximization behavior, it explained only a small fraction of matching behavior. These findings support the conclusion that probabilistic matching arises from the direct representation of probabilities rather than being a consequence of inferred rewards.

The proposed work analyzes the root structure of $E_8$ within a $56 \times 56 matrix framework. By leveraging a Gröbner basis of ideal equations, a system of recursive formulas is established to calculate the weights of $E_8$'s root structure. This study also examines additional relationships regarding $E_8$'s properties and explores potential connections between these results and the geometry of $E_8$'s Cayley plane.

This paper investigates the complexity of computing the Fréchet distance—a standard metric for assessing the similarity of polygonal curves—and presents the first algorithm capable of determining the Fréchet distance between two high-dimensional curves with a multiplicative approximation error of 2.

Measurement Error Mitigation (MEM) is a recently introduced technique designed to reduce the impact of readout errors in quantum computing. A MEM framework was developed to generalize this mitigation across an arbitrary quantum computer, applicable regardless of the specific readout error pattern. This approach accounts for readout errors occurring at any point within a quantum circuit, making it versatile for both full readout scenarios and those involving partial measurement.

Assisting humans with daily tasks is a primary focus of research in robotics. However, users often struggle to grasp how a robot interprets their teleoperated commands when a system lacks self-explanatory interface capabilities. To address this, a new framework is proposed that enables robots to articulate their control logic by emulating human explanations of button presses. By utilizing natural language, the system allows the robot to explain its interpretations of users' gestures. Drawing on data from human participants explaining button functions, the system learns how to generate these explanations. Furthermore, the system iteratively refines its explanations based on users' feedback, ensuring that explanations remain relevant to the specific user and the task.

The growing demand for capacity in future communication networks has spurred interest in advanced signal processing techniques, including 2-D arrays, array manifold learning, and machine learning. This paper provides a comprehensive review of current research regarding the application of machine learning to 2-D arrays and manifold learning specifically for 2-D array manifolds. We also explore the synergy between these two approaches, demonstrating that combining them offers significant potential. Key applications highlighted include 2-D hybrid beamforming, direction finding, channel estimation, and deep learning-based intelligent network architecture. Given the depth of existing work, this survey aims to equip researchers with the necessary context to advance the field. Finally, we identify critical research directions for future investigation in this rapidly evolving area.

Although X-ray computed tomography (CT) has become a standard diagnostic tool, its performance is often compromised by beam hardening and scattering artifacts. While single-energy sources are prevalent, polyenergetic alternatives offer advantages in speed and cost-efficiency. This study presents an end-to-end, data-driven deep learning framework designed to suppress both beam hardening and scattering artifacts in polyenergetic X-ray images. The proposed architecture employs a U-Net-based generator to produce a refined, physical image representation, utilizing a dedicated scattering simulation network as a complementary discriminator. A key innovation is the derivation of a novel loss function that leverages simulation-based scattering models to guide the training process. This approach eliminates the need for scarce, real-world scattered images typically required for supervised learning, enabling effective training entirely on clean, unsimulated data. Consequently, the framework offers a practical solution for enhancing polyenergetic CT without relying on annotated datasets acquired under scattered conditions.

This work investigates the propagation of light within a finite patch of metal using both local and non-local models. We find that while the local framework results in a divergence of the field at surfaces due to a delta-function susceptibility, inclusion of electron spill-out in a diffusive form provides regularization. This regularization allows the local model to accurately represent the physical system, ensuring that results from both non-local and modified local approaches align closely.

Although the benefits of integrating context into information retrieval are well-documented, determining the appropriate contextual words remains a challenge. While prior research has predominantly examined the selection of context using automated user profiles, our study shifts the focus to identifying context through active input from general users. Our findings demonstrate that context selected by these users significantly enhances retrieval performance. Specifically, user identification of context outperforms not only various automated selection strategies but also context provided by the same automated systems on query results, with significant gains observed particularly in shallow deep learning models. This evidence supports the conclusion that an active selection approach by users is generally more effective than fully automated systems.

This paper introduces a forecasting method designed to capture both seasonality and multiple long-memory characteristics in multivariate time series. While such data typically exhibits expected properties including seasonality, interdependence, and multiple sources of long memory, numerous existing models struggle to represent these patterns effectively. To address this, we propose a new hierarchical class of cointegrated models. Within this framework, each variable in the dataset is expressed as a linear combination, where the weights follow a specific parametric long-memory structure. By employing a factor model, we distinguish between latent long-memory common factors and idiosyncratic long-memory components. To ensure identifiability, we enforce a prior constraint on the common factors' long-memory structure. Our approach for estimating the entire model is developed using Maximum Likelihood, yielding estimators proven to be consistent and asymptotically normal. The methodology is validated through simulations and applied to real-world data, specifically forecasting US electricity prices. Results from this application demonstrate a notable reduction in Mean Squared Forecast Error (MSFE) compared to the baseline VARMA model.

Machine learning algorithms applied to Electronic Health Records (EHRs) hold significant promise for enhancing healthcare quality by addressing critical issues such as early disease detection, risk assessment, readmission prevention, and drug development through comprehensive data analysis. Despite these benefits, utilizing ML for this purpose remains challenging due to inherent data limitations, including incomplete entries, inherent uncertainties, and inconsistencies. To address these limitations, this study introduces a probabilistic representation for both structured and unstructured EHR data. It also presents a probabilistic mixed-membership hidden Markov model (pmHMM) designed to capture temporal patterns in multi-modal data while accounting for uncertainty and noise. The research validates the proposed pmHMM framework across three distinct applications: disease progression modeling, uncertainty analysis, various diagnostic tasks, and drug discovery. The results demonstrate that the pmHMM not only models disease trajectories with greater accuracy but also significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in solving these specific applications.

This work introduces a double continuum model that accounts for continuum solvent behavior and discrete ion effects, incorporating a non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation for the electrolyte's electrostatic potential, a nonlinear continuum dielectric boundary condition at interfaces, and a modified Debye-H\"uckel equation for a surface in direct contact with a specific ion species.

Automating the identification of requirements from textual data is a critical initial step in numerous natural language processing applications. While existing automated methods largely focus on extracting these requirements as named entities, they often overlook the contextual nuances essential for downstream tasks. This study introduces a novel approach that extracts requirements as graph nodes and links representing their relationships, utilizing graph neural networks (GNNs) and attention mechanisms. The method involves segmenting text into clauses and mapping them to a graph structure, followed by processing these data structures through a multi-task, multi-head, graph-based neural architecture. The neural model learns features by jointly identifying clauses, detecting clauses, predicting features, and inferring data relationships. Our results demonstrate that this proposed approach surpasses current state-of-the-art performance benchmarks.

This study examines the energy efficiency of maximum diversity network coding (MDNC) in contrast to a baseline scenario where network coding is absent. The findings indicate that adding network coding can boost energy efficiency by approximately 30%. Furthermore, the research derives the average end-to-end signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for both configurations within a multi-relay environment, comparing closed-form approximations against multi-hop outcomes.

We introduce a theory of Yu–Shiba–Rusinov (YSR) states that extends beyond traditional cases to include not only in-plane spin components within the superconducting surface's plane but also out-of-plane spin components that are generally oriented. By employing a Green's function approach, we examine a magnetically doped atom situated within a superconducting environment and identify a comprehensive set of formulas to describe their spectral signatures via a tunnel junction. Specifically, we derive an all-encompassing differential conductance model applicable to both standard Tunneling Spectroscopy experiments and those utilizing a spin-polarized tunnel probe. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between these experiments and existing theories to clarify the nature of YSR states and provide a thorough understanding of their characteristics under these conditions.

Distribution-to-distribution registration methods are now standard for aligning point clouds, yet they falter in the face of scale variations and dynamic elements. This paper introduces a temporal consistency regularization technique to constrain the impact of scene dynamics. By leveraging the understanding that object relative poses remain consistent across multiple frame pairs within a dynamic sequence, the approach effectively mitigates registration errors. We evaluate the proposed approach against Distribution-to-Distribution methods on the widely-used Dynamic Scene benchmark, achieving superior performance. Additionally, a novel point cloud registration framework, named "PRG," is introduced, combining Distribution-to-Reference methods with Distribution-to-Distribution strategies to maintain high accuracy across both static environments and dynamic, densely textured point clouds.

Satellite imagery is widely used across diverse sectors such as agriculture, cartography, and city planning. However, due to the vast volume of images involved, it is often difficult to manually locate specific objects within them. This paper introduces a new approach leveraging deep learning to automatically detect vehicles in satellite photos. The proposed system utilizes the Faster R-CNN framework, employing the popular ResNet50 architecture as its base feature extractor. To address the challenge of class imbalance in our dataset, we implemented random oversampling for minority classes and weighted the loss function by class. Additionally, to better represent the characteristics of vehicles captured in the imagery, we augmented the training data through rotation, flipping, color jittering, and affine transformations. Experimental results demonstrate that this method outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions, achieving a mean average precision (mAP) of 70.2% when evaluated on the COIN vehicle dataset.

Non-linear X-ray Absorption Near Edge Spectroscopy (XANES) is a phenomenon in which measured spectra rely on incident fluence, thereby encoding information about electronic dynamics. Decoding these fluence-dependent signals presents a significant challenge, as it demands a precise understanding of the specific electronic processes influencing spectral morphology. In this study, we introduce a new methodology that combines quantum metrology techniques with existing non-linear XANES theory to achieve this goal. Within this framework, the observed non-linear XANES response is modeled as a specific observable, allowing the technique to both identify the most effective detection methods for particular electronic processes and quantify those processes themselves through the measurement of their corresponding coupling constants. The method's utility is demonstrated by successfully distinguishing and measuring the light-matter coupling strengths associated with excitonic excitations and their subsequent relaxation. Furthermore, the approach offers a rigorous formalism for describing the higher-order contributions to the non-linear XANES signal that arise from many-body effects.

Although automatic modulation classification (AMC) utilizing Deep Neural Networks (DNN) has become a popular approach due to its superior performance, these models typically suffer from substantial increases in memory usage and computational complexity as a result of their deep architectures. This paper presents a novel method designed to mitigate both memory footprint and complexity within a DNN-based AMC framework. The work is structured in two parts. In the first, the proposed classification structure is built using a two-layer multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that relies on constellation symbols as input features. To reduce dependency on the specific characteristics of a given communication system, various statistical features are calculated to enhance robustness. In the second, the paper introduces a novel pruning technique aimed at reducing the number of weights within the neural network. The effectiveness of the overall approach is validated through simulations comparing proposed models against existing configurations.

Segmenting MS lesions in T1 MRI images is a difficult task for conventional deep learning methods because the small lesions are barely visible. In this paper, we introduce a novel multi-scale learning framework specifically designed to address these challenges. Our approach is a U-Net variant that incorporates multiple parallel convolutional paths within the encoder to extract multi-scale features. These features are then aggregated before being merged with corresponding deep layers in the decoder. Additionally, we have developed a specialized decoder that outputs probabilities for each pixel across all potential lesion classes. Experimental results confirm that our model achieves highly competitive segmentation accuracy, surpassing previous state-of-the-art techniques. The method is particularly effective at accurately delineating small lesions, which are otherwise difficult to detect.

The authors establish the differentiability of the optimal transport cost function within a compact domain of $C^2$ Riemannian manifolds, provided strict convexity holds. Their approach extends strongly convex transport results from Euclidean space, relying on a recent characterization of MTW conditions derived via Lagrange polynomials and partial Fourier transforms, alongside detailed analysis of random subspaces. Additionally, the authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the differentiability of an average optimal transport cost when random metrics are sufficiently concentrated around a base manifold.

This work addresses the issue of estimating parameters for ergodic continuous-time systems from time-series data. By applying the principle of maximum likelihood, we demonstrate that the corresponding continuous-time optimization is equivalent to a minimization of the H\"olderian energy functional. As the observation time $T$ approaches infinity, the model parameters are proven to converge to their true values with generalization error vanishing at a rate of $O(T^{-1/2})$. The study also presents a spectral approximation technique with an identified convergence order of $O(T^{-1} \log T)$, alongside a numerical example that validates these findings.

We conducted millimeter-wave continuum observations of IRDCs L182 and L182 using the ALMA instrument to investigate the relationship between stellar and protostellar mass within these structures. The survey detected a total of 183 sources, including 173 protostellar cores and 10 starless cores, by identifying a distinct separation in their mass distributions. Analysis reveals a log-normal probability density function for the mass distribution of starless cores, with a mean of approximately 1.8 solar masses, which is significantly lower than the distribution observed in protostellar cores (mean of approximately 4.1 solar masses). This finding suggests that the formation of stars in IRDCs is primarily driven by the collapse of sub-5 solar mass cores. Furthermore, the IRDCs exhibit a bimodal mass distribution at larger scales, with peaks centered at roughly 1.5 and 4.5 solar masses. This bimodal pattern aligns with theoretical models indicating that the gravitational instability of a filament is most likely to initiate collapse at these specific mass scales.

Primordial black holes (PBHs) are hypothesized to have formed in the early universe, comprising a potential fraction of the dark matter. This study explores the prospects of detecting such entities via gravitational microlensing, contingent on the assumption that they make up only a small portion of dark matter. We demonstrate that the microlensing data from the Fermi-LAT gamma-ray telescope retain significant power to constrain PBH abundance across mass ranges from 10 to approximately 100 solar masses ($M_\odot$). Furthermore, data from the EROS-II survey are utilized to limit PBH density for masses between 0.7 and 50 solar masses. Collectively, these findings indicate a complementary role for current observational datasets, covering nearly a full solar mass decade to enhance restrictions on dark matter attributed to primordial black holes.

Monodisperse molecules of a wedge-shaped design were subjected to molecular dynamics simulations to investigate their behavior under varying packing densities. At low packing densities (less than 0.5), the system exhibited a nematic phase, transitioning into a smectic A phase as packing density increased. Surprisingly, unlike typical amphiphilic systems, the packing density required for smectic A-nematic transitions varied significantly based on initial conditions. Simulations were further conducted to observe transitions between smectic A and isotropic phases, revealing that metastable smectic crystal structures could persist even beyond densities where such phases are no longer thermodynamically stable. Additionally, the study identified a metastable oblique smectic phase characterized by a tilted orientation relative to the smectic A layer, with its stability range also proving to be a function of initial conditions.

Parameter-efficient tuning focuses on adapting a small portion of pre-trained parameters, offering a cost-effective strategy for deploying cost-effective models. Conventional approaches, such as Prompt Tuning, address this by addressing the pre-trained model's encoder as a sequence-to-sequence task with implicit fixed prompts represented as categorical one-hot vectors. However, these methods struggle with tasks that do not align with sequence-to-sequence architectures, such as image classification or object detection. To address this, we present Prompt+Classifier Tuning as a new method that extends Prompt Tuning to non-sequential tasks. We achieve this by introducing a trainable classifier as a replacement for the standard linear head, allowing the model to learn task-specific features within a broader context. Furthermore, we analyze the relationship between our proposed method and previous techniques like fine-tuning, as well as prompt tuning, and provide empirical evidence that our method outperforms previous state-of-the-art results. Specifically, we evaluate the model on image classification tasks, including CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet, and ImageNet, as well as COCO detection.

This paper introduces a memory-inspired neural network paradigm designed to evaluate whether two collections remain equivalent following specific additions. To achieve this, we employ a recurrent set convolutional neural network (RCNN) that integrates two key components: a set convolutional layer capable of processing unordered set data, and a recurrent network endow the model with dynamic memory retention. This combination enables the architecture to effectively analyze the impact of items added to sets by leveraging its memory mechanism.

This study examines the interconnections among internal energy, enthalpy, and configurational entropy in polymer fluids. We establish linear relationships between these properties and the number of configurations in the polymer's internal state, as well as between entropy and a newly defined linear parameter representing the ratio of internal state configurations to external state configurations. Our analysis of the polymer fluid's internal energy yields results comparable to the lattice model findings of Leung and Cooper, which specifically linked internal energy to the number of configurations in the polymer. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these relationships satisfy the thermodynamic cycle and align with the findings of Leung and Cooper. Our findings indicate that the internal energy of the fluid is directly proportional to the internal energy of the polymer, while its enthalpy depends on the internal energy of the solvent. These conclusions support the view that the internal energy of the fluid arises from the sum of the internal energies of its polymer and solvent components.

It is widely acknowledged that even advanced transformer-based language models struggle with simple negation and other linguistic phenomena. This paper introduces the Multi-hold-on (MaHo) corpus to address the deficiency in existing data for testing how languages handle the connective nature of negation. MaHo consists of input-output pairs featuring 2D logical scenarios with objects that undergo multiple negations across the transitions. These sequences are automatically generated using the Logic In Numbers (LIN) framework and feature a distinct 2-to-1 mapping characteristic. Empirical results indicate that models trained on MaHo demonstrate significantly improved performance compared to those trained on LIN or other available data. Furthermore, models trained on MaHo achieve comparable results to those trained on LIN when tasked with reasoning about single negations, proving MaHo's utility in evaluating how languages handle the connective aspect of negation.

Attention mechanisms have established themselves as essential for Neural Machine Translation (NMT), yet they offer limited insight into how specific target words are actually constructed. This study examines a range of linear dependencies found in encoder-decoder architectures without introducing a new method. These findings allow for the creation of predictive models that infer how likely it is an neural machine translation system will generate a particular word based solely on the current context of already generated words. Finally, these results provide a novel, interpretable perspective on the NLM process that highlights the significance of lexical coherence.

This paper investigates the entanglement entropies across diverse configurations within conformal field theories defined in $d$ dimensions, specifically focusing on the large-$N$ limit of free and interacting models. For free scalar and spinor fields, a scaling behavior of $R^{\min(d, \text{effdim})}$ is identified, where the effective dimensionality depends on the field's spin; in particular, vacuum entanglement entropy on an $S^{d-2}$ sphere yields a non-vanishing result in large-$N$ free CFTs only when $d$ is odd. Regarding interacting models, we determine the universal coefficients of entanglement entropy on $S^1$ and $S^2$ for scalar fields using conformal perturbation theory, with outcomes that align perfectly at the fixed point and accurately reflect known deviations as one moves away from it.

This study utilizes continuous-time Markov chains to estimate Asian option prices. We introduce a new observation scheme that significantly streamlines the computation of semi-analytic Asian option prices. The method is demonstrated through a numerical example.

The nature of the diffuse gamma-ray background remains a longstanding unsolved issue in astrophysics. This study evaluates potential sources by analyzing recent data on galaxy clusters, superclusters, and quasars, while also considering other candidate objects. Our findings indicate that none of these entities, individually or collectively, can account for the observed diffuse gamma-ray background. Consequently, current evidence points toward an origin involving unresolved sources or sources yet to be discovered.

We examine a specific class of inflationary theories characterized by a non-minimal coupling between curvature and an inflaton field that undergoes oscillations. Our analysis of the full parameter space reveals two principal findings. Firstly, the nature of classical oscillations is crucial, and secondly, the curvature of potential at these oscillation points is of critical importance. Consequently, these features can be utilized to distinguish between competing inflationary models, as suggested by observational data.

Understanding the internal decision-making processes of visual models is crucial given their widespread adoption in various sectors. Since reliability hinges on trust, and interpretability fosters that trust, it has become a fundamental requirement. However, achieving meaningful interpretability remains difficult because there is no single standard definition, and existing approaches often fail to be consistent, reproducible, or aligned between their explanations and model behavior. In response, we introduce a framework designed to generate more reliable and consistently aligned interpretability outputs. First, it produces "local" (region-based) and "global" (whole-image) interpretations in a single forward pass. Second, it employs a dedicated loss function to rigorously assess these explanations and enable optimization for greater reliability. Third, it implements a data-driven, calibration-based strategy to ensure consistent quality. Experiments across diverse architectures, including CNNs, ViTs, transformers, and hybrid models, demonstrate that our method generates more consistent interpretations and creates a cohesive, unified interpretability pipeline.

Predictive models must manage inherent uncertainty, which Bayesian deep learning (BDL) aims to disentangle into aleatoric and epistemic types. While recent BDL frameworks have demonstrated efficacy across various domains, they frequently rely on computationally expensive approximate inference methods, such as variational Bayes or stochastic MCMC. These methods often compromise accuracy to achieve tractability, introducing potential biases in uncertainty estimation. This paper introduces a novel, efficient BDL framework for regression tasks. It incorporates a scalable sampling procedure capable of testing for the presence of either aleatoric or epistemic uncertainty in regression models. Furthermore, the proposed approach facilitates the training of Bayesian neural networks without the drawbacks associated with existing inference techniques. Extensive experiments conducted on both synthetic datasets and real-world benchmarks validate the robustness of this methodology.

The difficulty in modeling turbulent magnetic fields in astrophysical contexts is often bypassed by adopting a mean-field framework that represents the effects of turbulence via turbulent transport coefficients. These coefficients are calculated "in-situ" during dynamo simulations using the correlation method. This study examines the reliability of those coefficients derived from such simulations, focusing on a two-dimensional, magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) system with a magnetic quenching mechanism. Although the calculated coefficients consistently reproduce the dynamo $\alpha$-effect and exhibit stability over extensive timescales, they fail to capture variations in total dynamo activity when the strength of the quenching mechanism changes. This discrepancy stems from a substantial contribution of systematic errors, which dominate over random sampling errors in the correlation technique.

We report observations of the molecular outflow in NGC4945 using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array's CO J=2-1 line. The data reveal a plume of super-velocious gas moving eastward from the active galactic nucleus (AGN) with a physical velocity exceeding 100 km/s. This outflow exhibits distinct kinematic and spatial features, including blueshifted velocities, a double-peaked spectral profile, a slight position angle tilt, and a noticeable plume shape. Additionally, significant velocity shifts of up to 200 km/s exist between this outflowing component and the ambient quiescent gas. This case study demonstrates the Array's exceptional sensitivity and spatial resolution for resolving complex AGN-driven outflows. By comparing the mass loss rate against the accretion rate, the study finds an accretion-to-outflow ratio of approximately 98:2, indicating most of this outflow remains within 100 pc of the nucleus. This analysis highlights the critical role super-velocities play in regulating black hole growth and suggests this outflow could significantly impact star formation in the central region.

This work investigates the nonlinear phase mixing of an electromagnetic wave interacting with an electron beam in a magnetized plasma, specifically focusing on the resonant wave-particle effects described by the cold-fluid model. The analysis reveals that the time evolution of the distribution function converges to an exact analytical solution, a result confirmed by numerical simulations of the nonlinear Vlasov-Maxwell system. These solutions exhibit universal characteristics across diverse initial conditions. The non-resonant spectral energy density is observed to decay exponentially, with a rate determined solely by the detuning between the wave and particle frequencies. Furthermore, the study identifies a highly non-resonant universal phase portrait for the distribution function, which corresponds to a decaying modal structure. The findings are interpreted within the context of quasi-linear theory and nonlinear phase mixing, highlighting their complementary roles in describing the dynamics of wave-particle interactions.

Second Derivative General Linear Methods (SGLMs) are versatile frameworks capable of linearizing various nonlinear numerical integration schemes. In this study, we examine two specific nonstandard classes: the Linear Multistep Method corresponding to Case I and the Runge-Kutta method representing Case II. By applying these frameworks to the development of nonstandard SGLMs, we establish order conditions for methods of nonstandard types, revealing that SGLMs generally achieve a higher order of accuracy compared to their equivalent standard counterparts through the application of these schemes. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of implicit second-order cases (Case II) by constructing an implicit Runge-Kutta method of order 2 where the stages are determined by the linear system's second derivative. Finally, we demonstrate that these nonstandard classes also serve effectively as solvers for delay differential equations by applying them to a delayed test equation.

Portfolio performance is typically assessed relative to a benchmark, such as the Standard & Poor 500 Index, with the goal of outperforming it. This study introduces a novel method for determining optimal weights of assets relative to a specific benchmark using a Multi-objective Genetic Algorithm (MOGA). The primary objectives involve maximizing the excess return of the resulting portfolio relative to the benchmark and simultaneously minimizing exposure to risk. The study evaluates three distinct approaches: a single-objective optimization targeting the best possible benchmark outperformance, and two multi-objective optimizations that prioritize the first, second, or equal balance between outstanding performance and risk mitigation. The proposed methods are applied to data comprising 15 assets from the period of 2002 to 2017. The results demonstrate that all three strategies generate portfolios capable of outperforming the benchmark, with the first objective approach yielding superior returns and the two multi-objective approaches producing comparable outcomes.

Dwarf galaxies are among the most abundant systems in the cosmos, and their interstellar medium (ISM) is critical to understanding their evolution. This study presents a comprehensive, large-scale survey of the dwarf galaxy-hosting groups within 10 Mpc of the Milky Way, utilizing data from the VLA's ALFALFA project. The survey identified 10 dwarf galaxy candidates exhibiting neutral hydrogen (H I) signals. We conducted detailed observations of these candidates to determine whether H I signals originated from the dwarf galaxies themselves or from nearby foreground and background structures. Our results show that nine candidates are foreground or background interstellar gas clouds, while only one system, NGC 147, displays a clear H I signal attributable to the galaxy. The NG 147 signal is notably strong, with a high H I mass of 10^7.6 solar masses, representing the most massive H I detection in a Milky Way-proximate dwarf galaxy to date. This finding suggests a substantial reservoir of neutral hydrogen in NG 147, implying a high star formation potential.

Fermionic quasiparticles are proposed to exist at every node of the nodal line within a semimetal that possesses a nonzero axial charge. Our analysis indicates their stability against deviations from the semimetal phase, the axial charge being the critical factor that suppresses the bosonic excitations responsible for destabilizing the quasiparticles. This framework is applied to two systems: a theoretical model and the nodal-line semimetal pyrochlore MoTi$_3$O$_{12}$, with the latter showing a complete nodal-line network that spans the entire first Brillouin zone.

Lily, Nica, and Bell introduced the all-positive-cyclic structure on the free group, which led to a divergence theorem for the free group. In this paper, we establish a similar divergence theorem for the Thompson's groups $VA$ and $VA$, showing that they share the same local-to-local geometry. We also demonstrate a connection between our primary result and the concept of random Schanuel cycles.

This paper presents a streamlined, end-to-end version of Retriever-Augmented Generation (RAG) designed to efficiently resolve single-hop retrieval-based questions. By integrating a pre-trained language model with an in-filling architecture, our method eliminates the need for the labor-intensive pre-training phase required by the original RAG system. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach not only surpasses prior state-of-the-end methods but also delivers significant performance improvements. Additionally, we provide detailed analyses and visualizations to confirm that, despite sharing weights with models like BERT, our architecture successfully acquires the necessary reasoning capabilities.

This paper investigates orthogonal polynomials and their connection to quadrature rules under a generalised exponential-type logarithmic weight. We derive explicit formulas for the orthogonal polynomials and establish necessary and sufficient conditions under which these polynomials degenerate. Additionally, by determining optimal bounds for associated quadrature constants, we examine how these rules converge as the number of points increases.

Securing high-quality human labels from crowdsourcing sites like Amazon Mechanical Turk is a significant challenge, as output performance fluctuates with task difficulty, the demographic mix of workers, and the specific hiring strategies employed. This study introduces a novel, self-supervised algorithm designed to recruit workers from the Amazon Mechanical Turk platform specifically for Natural Language Processing datasets. The methodology operates by automatically generating gold answers and assessing label confidence based on the variability in individual worker outputs. We evaluated this approach on four datasets, including two from the GLUE benchmark, and demonstrated that our method effectively identifies potentially superior worker groups suitable for various dataset tasks.

This study introduces TS2-Net, a model designed for unsupervised anomaly detection and localization. It features a novel token shift module, which functions similarly to the cross-attention mechanism in self-supervised image patch discrimination tasks. By adaptively aligning an image's token representations with those of a reference, this method effectively captures long-range dependencies and facilitates robust anomaly detection. Furthermore, we establish the theoretical basis for integrating the token shift module into anomaly detection frameworks. Experiments on benchmark datasets confirm the approach's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The implementation is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/zhengzhu20/ts2-net}.

We introduce a simplified model featuring a leptophilic scalar that exhibits flavour-changing neutral currents within the top sector. Our analysis determines the model's viable parameter space alongside its most promising experimental discovery potential.

To analyze networks with multiple attachment mechanisms, we introduce a hybrid model that integrates uniform and preferential attachment. In this framework, new nodes join the network and connect to existing ones based on a probabilistic mixture: with probability $p$, links follow uniform attachment, while with probability $1-p$, they follow preferential attachment. Although uniform attachment alone generates a Poisson distribution for node degrees and pure preferential attachment creates a power-law distribution, our hybrid approach yields a novel hybrid distribution. We examine this distribution in detail, demonstrating that it retains the power-law characteristic of the preferential attachment phase while suppressing extreme values typical of that model. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the hybrid distribution allows distinguishing the underlying mechanisms, as the data can be fitted using either an hybrid model or a single attachment model with comparable goodness of fit.

This study addresses the challenge of mitigating wireless interference, with the aim of enhancing the performance of the next generation of wireless systems. We introduce a universal interference cancellation framework leveraging deep convolutional neural networks, applicable across diverse signal modalities, ranging from analog to digital and single or multi-carrier transmissions. The validity of our approach is demonstrated through simulations targeting an unlicensed 5G network operating in the 5.9 GHz ISM band, where interference arises from Non-Safety Cellular Broadcast (CSM) signals. Additionally, we evaluate the impact of network topology and channel conditions on neural network efficacy. The results indicate that the proposed method achieves a significant reduction in interference, boosting the signal-to-noise ratio by approximately 18 dB.

Quantum mechanics and general gravitational physics are the foundational theories for understanding the microscopic and macroscopic worlds, respectively; however, integrating them remains a significant unsolved challenge. In this study, we investigate the intersection of these domains by deriving the Schrödinger equation within a gravitational context using the Noether procedure. This results in the Schrödinger equation within a gravitational field, specifically a variant known as the Schrödinger-Pauli equation. This derivation reveals that gravitationally induced quantum effects are inherently non-linear, causing particles' energy levels to depend on their spin and charge. Consequently, highly precise experiments are required to observe these phenomena, with the non-linearity of gravitationally influenced quantum mechanics potentially offering a unique pathway to explore the nature of gravity at the Planck scale.

Countable locally standard measure algebras are characterized as pairs consisting of a locally compact space and a positive integer. In contrast, uncountable and non- $\sigma$-finite (up to null sets) such algebras are determined by three parameters: two cardinals and an integer. This paper demonstrates the existence of algorithms capable of constructing all such algebras and their isomorphisms. As a consequence, the set of all these algebras is well ordered by isomorphism.

Generalized parton distributions (GPDs) characterize the interplay between a nucleon's partonic momentum and transverse spatial localization. The extraction of these functions relies on elastic electron-ion collisions at the Electron-Ion Collider, where ion kinematics are constrained such that the ion remains intact and moves collinearly with the incoming electron. Under these elastic conditions, the relevant light-cone coordinates for nucleons remain unchanged in light-front quantization, whereas non-collinear transverse components do not. Consequently, the elastic constraint imposes restrictions on the Fourier coefficients of GPDs specifically in the $x^{\pm}$ direction, which correspond to light-front coordinates. However, in light-front coordinates, the $x^{\mp}$ directions are not constrained by the collision's elastic geometry. As a result, light-front transverse spatial relations do not yield constraints on GPDs, whereas the $x^{+}$ direction imposes constraints on the $x^{-}$ components and vice versa. These constraints are distinct from those found in other reference frames, such as light-front quantization or Milne coordinates, which yield different kinematic restrictions. Therefore, the extraction of GPDs from EIC data must be performed within a consistent framework that accounts for these specific constraint differences.

Every artificial intelligence (AI) system is vulnerable to errors, though its mistakes tend to differ from those of typically people. This paper investigates the nature of these discrepancies by conducting a large-scale study across the three most widely used datasets for objective error evaluation in image recognition benchmarks. Specifically, we analyze over 10 million predictions generated by both artificial intelligence models and human participants. The findings reveal that, across nearly every tested system, the majority of errors made by the AI mirror those of the human participants.

We examine the quantum phase transitions between superfluids and Mott insulators, as well as between superfluids and stripe insulators, occurring in square-lattice systems within the Mott-microemulsion model. These systems incorporate both nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor interaction terms alongside a spin-orbit Rashba coupling. By employing mean-field theory, we analyze the stable phases and corresponding order parameters. Our findings indicate that as the Rashba Rashba spin-orbit coupling increases, the critical interaction strength required for a superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition rises, whereas it decreases for a superfluid-to-stripe-insulator transition. Furthermore, numerical analysis reveals that these phase boundaries are largely unaffected by particle density when next-nearest-neighbor coupling is present, in stark contrast to the behavior observed in single-band models with only nearest-neighbor coupling. Additionally, phase diagrams are presented across a broad spectrum of parameters.

We explore various modes of group graphs degeneration and establish numerous findings with wider applications. This study demonstrates that group degeneration processes mirror those found in graphs, leading to the formulation of the Short-Long Exact Sequence (Short-Long EES). We demonstrate the applicability of this sequence by characterizing nontrivial examples of group cohomology, offering concrete cases where this approach yields meaningful results.
