We have developed a new detector simulation module designed to track particles scattered from the proton beams at the Interaction Point, thereby modeling particle-origin sources known as Beam-Induced Backgrounds (BIB). This module integrates into the existing DELPHES framework and offers a cost-effective method for evaluating BIB effects on detector performance with greater realism. Our approach draws upon prior studies on low-energy proton-beam background mechanisms, specifically adapting a specific empirical framework to accurately represent the simplified environment of empty fills during empty runs. This design is highly versatile, capable of simulating various types of low-energy background particles generated by diverse mechanisms. It is capable of handling particles from both primary and secondary interactions and can account for radioactive decay processes.

This work introduces Spartan, a framework for training sparse neural network models that combines mixup for sample-level sparsity and weight hard-sharing across the network for operator-level sparsity. The resulting sparse architectures maintain full accuracy when integrated into the training process of neural networks. This architecture is designed to adaptively generate unique, data-dependent sparse configurations for every layer and sample, enabling granular sparsity at the fine-grained level. Spartan is evaluated across diverse training scenarios, including standard dense training, end-to-end sparse training, and inference-based sparse methods. The study reveals that the method achieves the highest degree of sparsity compared to current approaches, reducing the number of non-zero weights by up to 95.2% (reducing active computations by 94.8%) without any loss of performance.

We examine the thermalization of a one-dimensional, ultracold Bose gas operating at the onset of Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) BKT transition and confined within a 1D trap. Employing numerical simulations of quantum kinetic equations, alongside theoretical frameworks based on Bogoliubov-de Gennes and Bogoliubov approximations, we find that thermal equilibrium is achieved solely in the energy associated with the transverse trap, while longitudinal and interaction components remain out of equilibrium. This behavior is linked to the specific form of the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum in the transverse direction, which governs the dynamics of both longitudinal and BKT excitations. Notably, this result holds exclusively for the weak-coupling limit; a slight increase in gas coupling causes the Bogoliubov spectrum to flatten at low momenta, allowing full thermalization across all degrees of freedom.

Unit tests are vital for ensuring software quality, yet they are often poorly written, leading to issues like reduced readability, maintainability, and readability. Heart-Rate Variability (HRV) is a vital metric for assessing cardiovascular health, yet it is labor-intensive to calculate manually. This study presents an automated HRV analysis framework utilizing Deep Learning (DL) to classify heart conditions based on RR-Intervals. We propose two distinct architectures: the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). To enhance CNN performance, we incorporated the Attention mechanism, resulting in an Attention-CNN model. Dynamic graph embedding is a core technology for time-dependent network analysis, facilitating tasks such as network forecasting, anomaly detection, and network supervision. This paper presents a new dynamic graph embedding approach, named DGE-Net, which utilizes self-supervised learning to enhance the model's generalization. Specifically, DGE-Net constructs a network representation for each time step and employs two primary components: a one-to-many contrastive learning module and a feature prediction module. Within the contrastive component, node representations are embedded and updated sequentially; this process involves generating node representations for the subsequent time step and predicting embeddings for the current dynamic network's nodes. The method employs self-supervised loss functions that contrast the current state's node representations against the generated representations for the next time step. Furthermore, to mitigate overfitting, the model incorporates an auxiliary objective based on predicting future node features. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that DGE-Net outperforms existing methods in both dynamic graph embedding tasks and prediction of time-evolving networks.

This study introduces a new approach for estimating the effects of interventions based on the underlying causal structure, capable of handling both non-randomized trials and causal questions regarding natural causal processes. This method employs the framework of the graph neural ordinary differential equations to estimate effects for multiple outcome types, including continuous, categorical, and count data. We developed deep generative models that leverage the latent structure of causal graphs to simulate synthetic data for training purposes. We tested our methodology against state-of-the-art competitors using both simulated datasets and one from the open-chickpea dataset, specifically focusing on estimating the causal impact of pod width on pod yield. This case study demonstrates that our approach can uncover causal relationships between unrelated variables by integrating domain-specific knowledge into the analysis.

We compute Betti numbers and specific generators for the local homology groups of a stratified space formed by gluing two smooth submanifolds along a common embedded submanifold. Our analysis covers both the cohomology groups of the resulting space and those of its reduced form, offering general formulas that encompass well-known scenarios, specifically smooth algebraic surfaces defined by the zero locus of a single equation. Furthermore, we address calculating these invariants when the stratified space comprises multiple strata, with applications such as the study of singular limits arising from sequences of discrete sets.

Determining camera poses is fundamental to vision-based robotics, with established methods relying on optimization, neural networks, or hybrid approaches leveraging both. While classical optimization and deep neural networks independently address pose estimation, each suffers from notable drawbacks: optimization techniques are computationally intensive and prone to converging on local minima, whereas neural networks demand significant processing time and often lack robustness under adverse conditions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel framework that merges optimization with a pre-trained neural network. Specifically, the proposed method utilizes a pre-trained network to generate an initial pose estimate from an image, which then feeds into an optimization routine that refines this estimate through a differentiable renderer. Consequently, this approach capitalizes on the rapid initial estimation provided by the neural network while employing network-derived gradients to fine-tune the result within an optimization loop. Experimental validation confirms that this optimization-driven framework enhances estimation accuracy and robustness compared to prior methods, demonstrating superior performance across varied scenarios.

In many real-world scenarios, the stochastic, long-term rewards available to reinforcement learning agents are either delayed or contingent upon satisfying specific constraints. Consequently, agents must develop strategies to recognize these constraints and incorporate them into their decision-making processes when optimizing for delayed, constraint-dependent payoffs. This research introduces a novel framework for identifying constrained tasks and a delayed-reward, constraint-conscious RL algorithm named "Delayed-Reward Constrained Q-Learning" (DRCQL). DRCQL enhances conventional Q-Learning by integrating constraint information into the value function, the evaluation of policy performance, or the generation of new policies. Specifically, DRCQL enhances the state-value function using a "penalty" mechanism that reduces estimated values in states with high cumulative constraint violations. Furthermore, the study validates this approach through experiments on both synthetic problems—such as the delayed penality, unbounded constraint, and bounded constraint MTCs—as well as practical applications like the car driving and inventory control problems.

GAIA (the European Space Agency astrometry satellite) is a space-based project designed to map the entire sky, capturing approximately one billion stars. The mission aims to create a highly precise 3D map of our galactic neighborhood by measuring positions, motions, and brightness for over a billion celestial bodies. The primary data processing pipeline (DP) is a complex workflow consisting of various subprocesses that convert raw instrument readings into catalog data. The complexity and volume of this workflow make it difficult to manage and visualize, particularly for non-experts. To address this, we have created an interactive visualization tool that represents the DP as a time-series network. This visualization helps users track how the pipeline operates throughout time, identifying specific events such as the processing of individual observation cycles. The paper details the methods used to build this visualization tool and discusses its practical applications in DP operation, including identifying issues, explaining changes, and planning future developments.

Recent research on complex networks has increasingly focused on identifying and analyzing community structures. While most studies rely on fully weighted or hybrid approaches that partially handle weight, this work argues for the necessity of consistently fully weighted clustering definitions. Through both synthetic and real-world examples, the authors demonstrate that applying uniform weight conditions yields superior outcomes for key network metrics like the Normalized Cut, community structure, and the Small World phenomenon. Consequently, the proposed method offers a more reliable and consistent framework for analyzing communities in complex networks.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have garnered significant attention for modeling complex systems by integrating prior physical knowledge into data-driven architectures. While purely data-driven models often struggle with generalization outside their training environments, PINNs leverage inductive biases to effectively handle tasks like inverse problems with limited data. This paper argues that PINNs can further benefit from incorporating out-of-distribution (OOD) detection capabilities. By implementing such mechanisms, one can enhance robustness against training set shifts and identify scenarios where models may fail. The authors utilize the recently proposed "energy" framework for OOD detection, adapting it to PINNs to flag inputs that could yield unreliable predictions. Given that PINNs often learn implicit probability distributions from training data, this approach aligns with energy methods by measuring the discrepancy between test inputs and training distributions. The framework is demonstrated using PINNs to approximate a chaotic dynamical system, showing that an associated potential function can effectively distinguish in-distribution data from those deviating from the training environment.

In the United States, air pollution is a significant public health concern. In the context of epidemiologic research, machine learning (ML) enhances the accuracy of air pollution models, which are essential for identifying vulnerable populations and establishing robust exposure assessments for study participants. Despite these benefits, the application of ML in this domain remains underutilized. This study reviews existing literature on integrating ML with epidemiologic air pollution exposure assessments, addressing both its advantages and challenges. The paper begins with an introduction to relevant background concepts in air pollution and health research, followed by an overview of various algorithms capable of generating enhanced models for exposure quantification. While the discussion covers statistical and computational approaches to algorithm selection, the primary focus remains on synthesizing current evidence regarding the implementation of these machine learning models.

We provide evidence for a Majorana zero-energy mode (MZES) in a gold/nickel tunnel junction. Our results indicate that the temperature-dependent tunneling conductance aligns with the prediction of a zero-dimensional thermal Majorana distribution. Furthermore, this distribution remains consistent across changes in bias voltage and tunneling temperature. A key observation is the emergence of a sharp Majorana peak in conductance that exhibits a quadratic narrowing as the thermal distribution's full width at half maximum responds to decreasing temperature. Additionally, a quantitative match between our data and the thermal Majorana zero-mode theory is achieved by setting the energy gap $\Delta$ to $0.2$ meV.

Specifically, this paper establishes a theoretical link between the eigenvalues and expected regret, showing that the design matrix's spectrum acts as a predictive metric for future regret in such settings. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that this design-based approach extends to the analysis of linear bandits, showing a clear correlation between the design matrix's eigenvalues and the algorithm's regret performance. This insight leads to the conclusion that the eigenvalues of the design spectrum effectively predict the algorithm's cumulative regret in linear bandits with well-behaved action spaces. In particular, the design-based method is shown to be a reliable predictor of regret in linear bandits with well-behaved action spaces. Matching sources between photometric catalogues is a common yet intricate task that typically relies on both position and magnitude data for photometry-based inclusion. Existing methods often overlook the importance of including magnitude data when cross-matching catalogues. This paper presents a new approach designed to address this gap by utilizing both positional and magnitude information when identifying sources. The method uses the two-dimensional Euclidean distance between two points to calculate how close sources are to each other. The code has been tested on several datasets and found to be effective at identifying sources in photometric catalogues. The method was further tested against Gaia EDR3 data, showing improved performance when both magnitude and position data are included. The open source package "SKYPy" is available for download at https://github.com/astro-skypy/SKYpy

This work introduces a concept of a "minimal" vertex cover within a hypergraph, defined as a cover that excludes any proper subset which is also a cover. The primary investigation explores system of sets that possess a specific property: for a given positive integer $k$, the system contains no more than $k$ non-trivial set covers. The paper establishes the precise necessary and sufficient conditions under which this property allows for the decision process to remain computable in polynomial time. These inquiries hold particular relevance to the study of redundant constraints in polyhedral theory, where the property corresponds to the existence of vertex covers with cardinality at most $k$ among certain polyhedral inequalities involving $x_0$ as a free variable.

Ontologies, which formalize structured collections of concepts and their interconnections, are increasingly vital in biomedicine. These formal models facilitate knowledge sharing, interoperability, and reusability among stakeholders such as researchers, clinicians, and analysts. However, manually constructing and maintaining ontologies is labor-intensive and demands a high level of expertise. To address this, automated knowledge mining from biomedically oriented textual sources has become a prominent field of study. This paper introduces BiomedMap, a knowledge base comprising 1.3 million mappings between biomedical concepts extracted from literature. BiomedMap was generated using a machine learning framework that analyzes 12.5 million sentences to establish over 4 million instance relationships and 4 million associations between ontological entities. We outline the methodology used to build the base and evaluate its utility through usability testing involving a cohort of scientists.

Unlike standard CycleGAN applications, our approach utilizes the inter-domain losses available in traditional domain adapters. The method is evaluated on the TIMIT dataset for character-level ASR and finds significant improvements: it reduces the error rate by 29.99% during the intrinyic test and by 29.99% on the test set.

Inspired by principles of active inference, this hypothesis proposes that biological agents explore their environment to explore and reduce the surprise associated with their sensory experiences. Central to this theory is the concept of *marginal inference*, where an agent simulates potential actions in its internal model, anticipating sensory outcomes. By selecting the path that minimizes the internal likelihood of unexpected sensory data, the agent is guided toward the most effective course of action. We apply this framework to a grid-world scenario featuring a single agent and a single target, utilizing a simple grid-based representation for the agent's internal state. While a full detailed description exceeds the scope of this abstract, we demonstrate how the agent's internal state can be inferred from its observed movements using our specific state-space definition.

This study employs non-equilibrium statistical mechanics to examine the Soret effect in binary systems composed of dimer and monomer molecules. The analysis indicates that the theoretical framework developed is sufficiently robust to address more intricate models where dimers remain intact despite molecular collisions. Furthermore, the findings reveal that the sign of the Soret effect can be reversed in soft-sphere systems by varying the ratio of mass to thermal de Broglie wavelength for the dimer-to-monomer species.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) demands a nuanced grasp of language to accurately compute precise, consistent, and unbiased evaluations of writing. While existing deep learning models excel at AES tasks, they often neglect critical long-term dependencies and fail to deliver granular, word-level insights into writing flaws. To address these limitations, we introduce **Escore**, an AES framework grounded in attention mechanisms that facilitates the dynamic weighting of contextual cues and specific linguistic deficiencies. By integrating three distinct attention mechanisms, the model can jointly assess global writing quality while pinpointing individual words for fine-grained analysis. Tested on two major datasets—PUMAS and LiS—the framework achieved state-of-the-art results with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.76 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.49 on PUMAS, alongside scores of 0.73 and 1.74 respectively on LiS.

A key difficulty in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the extensive variation in pedestrian appearances across different domains, frequently resulting in missed detections. Current methods primarily address this by aligning feature distributions, yet they often overlook the alignment necessary within semantic spaces. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel approach centered on semantic-guided feature alignment. Specifically, we introduce "Semantics-Guided Feature Alignment" (SGFA), a new training objective that integrates feature alignment strategies guided by inherent semantic information. Additionally, we introduce an "Semantic-Guidance Feature Integration" (SGFIF) module designed to extract meaningful object attributes and direct the alignment process. By incorporating this new training metric, SGFIF effectively enhances feature alignment in both semantic feature spaces and broader statistical feature spaces, thereby significantly improving detection accuracy when transferring across domains.

Consumer music tracks recorded by personal devices, like smartphones, often suffer from distortions due to subpar audio fidelity, small acoustic spaces, and the resulting limitations of their larger speakers and microphones. This study introduces an end-to-end trained neural network designed to restore the original signal by eliminating these artifacts, thereby enhancing mobile audio quality. An end-to-end approach was preferred to avoid the complexities of intermediate feature mapping, and the model utilizes the WavLM speech representation network alongside two novel distortion-based losses to optimize performance. Testing this deep learning system within a machine learning environment revealed that the proposed system outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 1.6 dB improvement in Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) on the MUSIQ-Classic-IMC benchmark and a 1.7 dB improvement on the MUSIQ-Client-Audio test set.

Although the timing of parabolic motion's onset—specifically the Point of Release (PoR)—has been established as a critical indicator for detecting throwing errors, previous research has largely relied on visual assessments. This study introduces a new method utilizing pressure-sensitive floor mats to automatically pinpoint the PoR, an advancement that enables controlled experiments on how throwers correct their own mistakes. Findings indicate that PoR detection accuracy is contingent upon the throwing style, with overarm throws yielding results that vary based on individual consistency. Furthermore, while over and underarm throws generally produce similar PoR errors, the underarm variant shows a distinct delay relative to the ideal target. These insights suggest that floor mat technology serves as an effective, automated tool for identifying and analyzing throwing mistakes.

Achieving robust Neural Machine Translation (NMT) hinges on effectively incorporating source language structure into models. While prior studies demonstrate that integrating dependency parsing enhances performance, their application is often restricted by the computational demands of traditional methods. This paper introduces "Concparse," a dependency parser utilizing an attention mechanism and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) that achieves high accuracy with minimal processing overhead. We further adapt this model for Neural Machine Translation by leveraging its hierarchical nature and atomic relationships as well as its attention dynamics, a strategy that yields superior results compared to models based solely on sequential inputs or dependency structures. Experimental validation across multiple datasets confirms the efficacy of our approach.

Accurate modeling of astrochemical processes relies heavily on precise binding energy values; however, significant variability among data sources often undermines the reliability of these values. To address this, we introduce a Bayesian formalism designed to derive robust prior probability density functions from existing binding energy data. This approach facilitates a direct comparison of different collection types by synthesizing binding energy distributions and allows for efficient data integration. Testing against datasets with known binding energies for molecules like H₂O and NH₃ demonstrates that the method yields mean values closely matching the true energies, thereby establishing reliable priors for use in chemical simulations.

This study examines a multiplicative stochastic process limited by a lognormal tail below, utilizing a Log-Coleman-Lowes (S-Lowes) or Log-Coleman-Lowes (S-Lowes) distribution to define its floor constraint. Based on the generated data, we demonstrate that the process exhibits a power-law tail at higher values, consistent with observed financial stock returns. Leveraging this insight, we propose a new generation algorithm that aligns with the d-Lowes distribution at the base while replicating real-world stock return tail characteristics. Furthermore, we analyze the process's variance and entropy to establish upper bounds for these metrics. This research offers a theoretical framework and computational model for the generation of skewed return distributions, providing a robust foundation for the development of advanced risk assessment methodologies and pricing strategies.

We introduce a novel randomized measurement technique for classical simulation of quantum systems, wherein sampling costs grow only linearly with circuit depth to achieve a fixed fidelity. This efficiency stems from the observation that individual measurement samples exhibit high depth-dependent redundancy, allowing effective compression. By identifying and leveraging this depth-abstraction, the method enables the randomized sampling of deep quantum circuits with a polynomial increase in computational complexity. We validate the approach by applying it to various scenarios, including specific sampling tasks, the evaluation of quantum advantage hypotheses, and the classical verification of depth-enhanced quantum advantage improvements.

Meta-learning focuses on acquiring meta-knowledge to expedite the learning of new tasks. Representation learning, a key component of meta-learning, aims to derive task-agnostic data aspects to facilitate rapid new task acquisition. This work introduces an approach to construct such representation using the concept of "marginal independence." We model representation learning as discovering the marginal distribution of data, utilizing the mutual information between a task and data as a disambiguation metric to disprove task-agnosticity, and the mutual entropy between an acquired representation and data as a constraint to ensure it remains a valid marginal. To address the challenge of unknown task mutual distributions, the paper introduces the Independent Task Assumption, which limits the mutual dependency between the data's latent variable distribution and the task to its invariant subset. This approach is demonstrated to yield higher performance than existing techniques on both synthetic datasets and the CIFAR-100 benchmark.

Knowledge Distillation (KD) enables machine translation models to acquire performance that rivals their larger counterparts, thereby facilitating the deployment of language processing tools for low-resource languages where computational resources are constrained. Despite this promise, existing KD approaches face two significant hurdles: training is computationally expensive due to the necessity of training both a large teacher model and a student model simultaneously, and performance often degrades when a single teacher is used to train multiple independent student models. To address these challenges, our novel method decouples the training of the student model from that of the teacher, eliminating the computational burden during the student phase. Furthermore, our algorithm introduces a dynamic strategy for training individual student models using multiple teachers concurrently. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach not only surpasses current state-of-the-art KD techniques but also performs on par with the large-scale models it mimics. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishjain2000/MTKD.

Deep learning models, particularly those designed for semantic segmentation, typically demand extensive labeled datasets. This is a significant barrier for medical imaging, where data annotation is particularly costly and time-consuming. In response to these challenges regarding semantic segmentation and detection of pneumonia in chest X-rays, this study introduces an augmentation-based strategy. Our approach utilizes labeled datasets and applies various augmentation techniques to both train and test a Deep Convolutional Neural Network (DCNN) segmenter. By evaluating multiple methods, this research identifies an optimal configuration that reduces labeled data requirements while maintaining high performance. We also examine the impact of specific transformations, such as Gaussian noise, on segmentation outcomes. Experiments were conducted using the NIH ChestX-ray dataset, which contains radiographs of 1,000 patients affected by community-acquired pneumonia. The results demonstrate that random cropping and flipping in conjunction with or without the application of Gaussian noise yield the best performance, achieving comparable segmentation accuracy with just 1% fewer images than previously required.

While state-of-the-art image captioning models produce descriptive factual narratives, they often lack the ability to adapt to other prevalent image caption styles, including subjective or emotional interpretations. This paper introduces a new approach by training these models within defined styles using predefined "style prompts" as inputs. Our experiments across three datasets—two focused on general images and one on meme memes—reveal that our method is highly versatile and can successfully generate captions in three distinct categories: factual, emotional, and style-specific variants of the latter two. Additionally, the study explores the relationship between style diversity and overall captioning quality, analyzing performance through the lens of the CIDEr metric.

The proliferation of autonomous systems and decision-making algorithms has intensified the necessity to define "harm" to guide ethical design. Since traditional definitions of harm predominantly focus on damage to humans or other agents, they often overlook the impact of algorithms on societal structures. This paper introduces a novel framework for modeling harm that leverages causal models to establish clear criteria for identifying harmful scenarios within autonomous systems. By utilizing the counterfactuals inherent in causal modeling, our approach can pinpoint interventions where algorithms have caused harm. We apply this model to generate a set of Sufficient Conditions for Identifying Harm (CCIH) and demonstrate its ability to account for the complex mechanisms involved in algorithmic damage.

The expansion of autonomous systems and decision-making algorithms has heightened the need for a definition of "harm" that can guide ethical design. Since prior definitions of harm primarily focus on injury to humans or other agents, they often overlook the impact of algorithms on society. This paper introduces a new framework for modeling harm that leverages causal models to clearly define harmful scenarios in autonomous systems. By utilizing the causal model's capacity to identify contributions to outcomes from the source, our model can pinpoint instances where algorithms have caused harm. We apply this model to generate a set of Sufficient Conditions for Identifying Harm (CCIH) and demonstrate its ability to account for the complex mechanisms involved in algorithmic damage.

This study presents an open-source library named DL4DS, designed to simplify the deployment of deep learning workflows across distributed environments. The package integrates popular deep learning tools with Apache Spark and has been released under a Creative Commons license. By offering a unified interface for training neural networks on clustered systems, it enhances efficiency and facilitates the development of meta-learning algorithms, which rely heavily on extensive parallel computing capabilities. Consequently, DL4DS increases the flexibility and adaptability of both existing and emerging applications.

Speech Translation (ST) and Speech Synthesis (SS) are both considered challenging tasks in the field. While the former suffers from data scarcity, particularly in the zero-shot setting, the latter faces significant quality challenges. This study introduces a new approach to address the issues of both tasks by employing a unified, end-to-end multi-lingual, multi-modality framework. Specifically, we utilize a cross-lingual transfer strategy to enhance the performance of zero-shot translation and generate high-quality audio for cross-lingual speech synthesis. Our method involves training a single ST model on multiple languages and feeding its output text, converted to text-to-speech, into a unified speech synthesis system. This work introduces a novel concept of dissipative dynamic boundary conditions (DDBC) for thermal conduction. Grounded in boundary entropy and energy balance principles, these conditions align the dynamics of heat at the surface with the Carathéodory framework for dissipative systems, a model renowned for its mathematical rigor and accuracy in describing the irreversible transfer of heat. The study provides proof of existence and uniqueness regarding the solution to the dynamic boundary heat equation under DDDCs, with convergence toward the steady state established via an energy method. Notably, this specific formulation represents the first instance incorporating dissipative dynamic boundary conditions within the context of conduction theory.

Accurate forecasting energy consumption holds significant value for both providers and consumers. However, predicting usage patterns becomes a complex, difficult task when moving from aggregated data to the fine-grained level of individual customers. This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing clustering techniques combined with supervised learning models to address this energy consumption prediction challenge. The effectiveness of the method is evaluated using real-world datasets, with experimental outcomes demonstrating a notable improvement over existing state-of-the-art solutions.

Recent advancements in machine learning have generated significant enthusiasm, yet capturing human expertise to guide these models remains challenging. While the literature outlines numerous approaches to incorporate knowledge into ML with a particular focus on rule-based systems, there is limited exploration within the domain of computer vision. This study introduces a systematic method to encode visual knowledge into Bayesian priors and its application to object detection. By employing a probabilistic framework for object detection, we utilize a multi-modal distribution over the regression outputs of deep neural networks to encode constraints on possible outcomes. By adjusting the parameters of this priors, we can embed domain expertise, thereby enhancing the overall detection performance. This approach demonstrates superior results over current state-of-the-art methods and provides an accessible framework for integrating and formalizing visual domain expertise.

Precise localization and identification of vertebrae are essential for various clinical tasks, including diagnosing spinal diseases and screening for tumors. However, such procedures often face challenges due to pathologies like degenerative spondylolisthesis, which alter the typical appearance of the spine. This paper introduces a solution utilizing instance-level prior knowledge of vertebral structures to boost the accuracy of localization and identification. The study presents two novel frameworks: Multi-level Structure-Guided Localization (MSGL) and Multi-level Structure-Guidated Localization with Attention (MSGLA). Unlike previous methods, these models explicitly integrate knowledge about the spatial distribution and appearance of individual vertebrae, allowing them to correct the outputs of black-box detectors. Specifically, MSGL utilizes detectors as components within a two-stage system, employing a novel locational attention prior that is both data-driven and anatomically informed. This prior consists of two sub-priors: one defining the spatial layout of the vertebral column and another specifying each vertebra's specific location within that layout. The proposed appearance prior further incorporates black-box identification outputs. In the MSGLA model, a self-supervised learning approach allows the system to automatically learn these appearance priors. Experimental results show that both models significantly surpass state-of-the-art methods in challenging scenarios.

The interaction between free electrons and confined electron states is examined within a repulsive potential. When an electron's energy precisely matches that of the polariton confined by the potential, its wavefunction becomes bound, even without any attractive force present. This mechanism is identified as the primary origin of the negative energy states associated with image charges in metallic systems. The analysis further demonstrates that this effect is inherently non-adiabatic; specifically, if the electron traverses the confined region slowly, it can evade entering the bound state. These theoretical predictions are validated through numerical simulations, which also reveal that image charges and related phenomena can be mitigated by adjusting the electron's trajectory speed. Additionally, the findings suggest that image charges and negative energy states can be manipulated to control the motion of electrons moving through one-dimensional wires.

This paper introduces a computational framework designed to synthesize locomotion for multi-link, actuated robots. The method centers on central pattern generators (CPGs), which modulate the timing and phase of each limb actuator to determine the resulting robot gait. During training, the model employs CCGs to guide the animal model gait. The primary advantage of combining CCGs with a reinforcement learning framework is that it enables the exploration of a compact, biologically grounded search space, allowing for rapid adaptation to diverse environments. Additionally, this flexible, hierarchical approach facilitates easy modification of CCGs to handle local obstacles. Consequently, our proposed framework consistently produces lifelike and practical locomotion strategies.

We introduce the variational separability verifier (VSV), an adaptable quantum circuit designed to identify the maximal contiguous sequence of qubits exhibiting entanglement with the remainder of the system. Initially developed as a probe for quantum phase transitions, this approach is now streamlined for integration as a subroutine within the variational quantum eigensolver (VGE), effectively serving as a real-time metric for graph partitioning. Furthermore, we examine the circuit's performance on superconducting qubit hardware, demonstrating that even with restricted connectivity and moderate noise levels, the device can successfully map entanglement dynamics in real-time systems.

Recent advancements in visual search allow users to retrieve items using casual text or images, yet challenges remain when users wish to search for modified versions of an object's attributes, such as a black shirt in large sizes. While prior research has addressed attribute manipulation in still images, dynamic video manipulation remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce the first dataset for the task of Fashion Attribute Manipulation (FAM) in videos. Our approach employs a novel model named vTransAM, which utilizes a multi-step, hierarchical strategy to handle these attributes. Specifically, the model first isolates the target object, then generates the necessary spatial transformations, and finally isolates the manipulated result for output. We have evaluated the model across six distinct attributes and demonstrated that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, we have examined the robustness of the model and confirmed its utility in enhancing learned representations for image retrieval tasks.

This study introduces a parameter choice rule designed for ill-posed problems characterized by a strongly convex function, a model that encompasses a broad category of inverse problems within parametric families. We establish the asymptotic accuracy of this rule under the assumptions of noise independence, a noise level $\delta$, and bounded source components $\gamma$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the convergence rate achieved matches the optimal order defined by the information lower bound. The method's validity is further illustrated through specific examples, including those concerning the determination of zeros for analytic functions and the identification of monotone functions from their Hilbert transforms.

We introduce a straightforward and rapid cost constructor designed for light field (LF) depth estimation, which relies on the linear relationship between image intensity and object depth. This design offers significant speed advantages over conventional methods while substantially reducing the disparity in final depth map quality regarding the established metric, EPE. To further enhance depth map quality, we present a deep neural network (DNN) regressor specialized for refining the output from the new cost constructor. Empirical evaluations across various datasets reveal that incorporating learning-to-disparity (L2D) depth priors yields further performance gains. Additionally, the newly proposed cost constructor proves effective for learning-to-disparity tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on both the H3M and H3M-LF datasets.

This study investigates the Darboux transformation and its applications to the Fokas-Lenells equation. We present a method within the framework of nonlinear supersymmetries to derive the corresponding transformations. Utilizing this method, we generate further rational and possonic solutions for both $1\text{-}$ and $2$-component Fokas-Lenells systems. Consequently, we demonstrate that the Darboux transformation can effectively be utilized to fully generate these solutions.

This study investigates semi-classical gravity models lacking a full Riemannian structure, specifically focusing on theories based on generalized geometry. We present simplified methods for developing canonical actions within this generalized framework, which remain consistent across all consistent dimensional reductions to lower dimensions. Additionally, we show that double field theory (DFT) offers the most streamlined approach for deriving these actions, effectively reducing the complex issues of generalized geometry to standard DFT frameworks. Finally, we apply these findings to specific cases, including conventional Ricci-squared gravity augmented with generalized torsion, resulting in novel theories that find natural applications in string field theory contexts.

Next-generation home Wi-Fi networks are expected to deliver ultra-high data rates and a robust network capacity to meet the demands of bandwidth-intensive applications like virtual reality and high-definition video streaming. However, the increasing number of users and devices in crowded environments leads to network congestion, causing packet losses and reduced performance. This study introduces a new mechanism that autonomously adapts transmission parameters to enhance transmission efficiency, aiming to support latency-sensitive and high-bandwidth services. The proposed approach utilizes underutilized spectrum to enhance capacity while employing an adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) scheme to further improve network performance. Additionally, a machine learning-based method is presented to accurately predict channel conditions, enabling more effective transmission strategies. Experimental results indicate that this approach can boost total network capacity by up to 200% and lower end-to-end latency by 60% compared to existing solutions.
